about: The scripted AI lesson for p1-energy-stores (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. The first lesson of P1, so there are no recall questions from earlier lessons.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about energy: the ways it can be held in things, how it moves from one place to another, and why some of it always ends up where nobody wanted it.
Energy is what is needed to make things happen: to make things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy itself, but you can see what it does.
Energy is measured in joules, written J. One joule is a small amount: lifting an apple from the floor onto a table takes about 1 J.
Energy can be held in an object in different ways, called energy stores. There are eight of them, each with its own name. They come one at a time.
First, the kinetic store: the energy of anything moving. A car on the road, a kicked ball and a running person all have energy in their kinetic store.

steps.question: A football is lying still on the grass. Does it have energy in its kinetic store?
steps.right: You've got it: the ball is not moving, so its kinetic store is empty, however heavy it is.

wrong.other: Not quite: the ball is not moving, so its kinetic store is empty.
wrong.heavy: Not quite: being heavy does not matter. The kinetic store is only for moving things, and the ball is lying still, so its kinetic store is empty.
wrong.could: Not quite: it might move later, but right now it is still, so its kinetic store is empty.

idk.hint: Kinetic is the store for moving things. Is the ball moving?

steps.answerWhy: Only moving things have energy in their kinetic store, so a ball lying still has none.

steps.text: Second, the gravitational potential store: the energy of anything raised up. A book on a high shelf, or a roller coaster at the top of a hill, has energy in its gravitational potential store.
Third, the elastic potential store: the energy of anything stretched or squashed. A stretched spring and a squashed rubber ball both have energy in their elastic potential store.

steps.question: Someone stands still on a trampoline, and its surface is pulled down under them. Which store holds energy in the trampoline?
steps.right: Yes: elastic potential. The trampoline is stretched, and stretched things have energy in their elastic potential store.

wrong.other: Not quite: elastic potential, because the trampoline is stretched.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: elastic potential. Nothing is moving while the person stands still, so the kinetic store is empty. The trampoline is stretched, and that fills its elastic potential store.
wrong.gravity: Not quite: elastic potential. The trampoline has not been lifted higher; it has been stretched downwards, and that fills its elastic potential store.

idk.hint: The trampoline surface is stretched. Which store is for stretched or squashed things?

steps.answerWhy: The trampoline is stretched, so the energy is in its elastic potential store.

steps.text: Fourth, the thermal store, which depends on how hot something is. Every object has some energy in its thermal store. A hot cup of tea has more than the same tea once it has gone cold.
Fifth, the chemical store: energy held in food, in fuels such as wood and coal, and in batteries. Burning a fuel or digesting food releases it.

steps.question: Which of these has a lot of energy in its chemical store?
steps.right: Yes: petrol is a fuel, and fuels hold energy in their chemical store.

wrong.other: Not quite: the full tank of petrol. Fuels hold energy in their chemical store.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: the full tank of petrol. A spinning wheel is moving, so its energy is in its kinetic store.
wrong.thermal: Not quite: the full tank of petrol. A hot radiator's energy is in its thermal store, because it is hot.

idk.hint: Food, fuels and batteries fill the chemical store. Which button is a fuel?

steps.answerWhy: Petrol is a fuel, and fuels hold energy in their chemical store.

steps.text: The last three. Everything is made of tiny particles called atoms.
The centre of each atom is called its nucleus. More than one nucleus are called nuclei.
The nuclear store is the energy held in the nuclei of atoms.
Nuclear power stations release it from uranium fuel by splitting nuclei apart. The Sun releases it in its core.
Rub a balloon on your hair and it becomes charged, which means it carries static electricity. A charged balloon can stick to a wall.
The electrostatic store is the energy between charged objects, like a charged balloon and your hair, or a thundercloud and the ground.
And the magnetic store: energy between magnets, or between a magnet and a piece of iron.
All together, there are eight stores: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic and magnetic.

steps.question: Two magnets are held a little apart, then let go, and they snap together. Which store did their energy come from?
steps.right: Yes: magnetic. The energy was held between the magnets, in their magnetic store.

wrong.other: Not quite: magnetic. The energy was held between the magnets.
wrong.static: Not quite: magnetic. Electrostatic is for charged things like a rubbed balloon; these are magnets.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: magnetic. Nothing is stretched or squashed; the energy was held between the magnets.

idk.hint: Both objects are magnets. Which store is named after magnets?

steps.answerWhy: The energy was held between the magnets, in their magnetic store.

steps.question: A skier waits, not moving, at the top of a tall slope. Which store holds energy because of the skier's height?
steps.right: Yes: gravitational potential. Anything raised up has energy in its gravitational potential store.

wrong.other: Not quite: gravitational potential, the store for things that are raised up.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: gravitational potential. The skier is not moving yet, so the kinetic store is empty. Being high up fills the gravitational potential store.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: gravitational potential. Nothing is stretched or squashed. Being high up fills the gravitational potential store.

idk.hint: The skier is high up and not moving. Which store is for raised things?

steps.answerWhy: Anything raised up has energy in its gravitational potential store.

steps.text: Energy can move from one store to another. Watch what happens to a ball thrown straight up: it slows down as it rises.

steps.question: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top it stops for a moment. Where has the energy from its kinetic store gone?
steps.right: Yes. As the ball rose, its kinetic store emptied into its gravitational potential store. That is why it can fall back and speed up again.

wrong.other: Not quite: into its gravitational potential store, because the ball is now higher up.
wrong.gone: Not quite: energy does not vanish; it moves to another store. As the ball rose and slowed, the energy moved from its kinetic store into its gravitational potential store.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: nothing is stretched. The ball is higher up, so the energy went into its gravitational potential store.

idk.hint: As the ball rises, it slows down but gets higher. Which store grows as something gets higher?

steps.answerWhy: The ball is higher up, so its kinetic store emptied into its gravitational potential store.

steps.prompt: In one line: which store fills up when something moves faster, when it is lifted higher, and when it is stretched?
points: gravitational potential when it is lifted higher
elastic potential when it is stretched
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: moving faster fills the kinetic store, lifting higher fills the gravitational potential store, and stretching fills the elastic potential store.

keyPoints.heading: The four ways energy is transferred

steps.text: Next: how energy gets from one store to another. Moving energy from one store to another is called transferring it.
There are four ways to transfer energy, called pathways.
The first pathway: mechanically, by a force. When you kick a ball, the push of your foot transfers energy into the ball's kinetic store.
The second: electrically. When a battery is joined to a lamp by wires, a flow of electricity called a current passes round the wires, and it carries energy to the lamp.
The third: by heating, which means energy passing from a hotter object to a cooler one, like from a hot drink into your cold hands.

steps.question: You hold a cold can of drink, and your hand gets colder. Which way is energy going?

options.text: From your hand to the can, by heating
From the can to your hand: the cold flows in

steps.right: Yes: your hand is hotter, so energy passes from your hand to the can by heating. Your hand gets colder because it is losing energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: from your hand to the can, by heating, because your hand is hotter.
wrong.cold: Not quite: cold is not something that flows. Energy passes from the hotter thing to the cooler one: from your hand to the can. Your hand feels colder because it is losing energy.
wrong.none: Not quite: your hand gets colder, so it is losing energy. It goes from your hand to the cooler can, by heating.

idk.hint: Heating always moves energy from the hotter object to the cooler one. Which is hotter, your hand or the can?

steps.answerWhy: Your hand is hotter, so energy passes from your hand to the can by heating.

steps.text: The fourth: by radiation, which means waves such as light and infrared. Infrared is the invisible warmth you feel from a fire or the Sun. Things that take in light or infrared get warmer.

steps.question: A phone is charging. Energy from the plug reaches the phone through the cable. Which pathway carries it?
steps.right: Yes: electrically. A current in the cable carries the energy to the phone.

wrong.other: Not quite: electrically, by a current in the cable.
wrong.mech: Not quite: electrically. Nothing is being pushed or pulled by a hand or a moving part; the energy travels by a current in the cable.
wrong.rad: Not quite: electrically. Radiation is light and infrared waves; through a cable, the energy goes by a current.

idk.hint: A cable carries a current. Which pathway uses a current?

steps.answerWhy: A current in the cable carries the energy to the phone, so the energy goes electrically.

steps.text: To describe a transfer in one sentence, name the pathway, the store the energy leaves and the store it goes into.

For a car braking, the sentence is: energy is transferred mechanically, by the force of the brakes rubbing on the wheels, from the kinetic store of the car to the thermal store of the brakes. The brakes get hot.

steps.question: An apple falls from a tree. Fill the gap: energy is transferred mechanically, by the pull of gravity, from the apple's ___ store to its kinetic store.
steps.right: Yes: gravitational potential. The apple starts high up and ends up lower and moving.

wrong.other: Not quite: gravitational potential. The apple starts high up, and falling empties that store into its kinetic store.
wrong.chemical: Not quite: gravitational potential. The apple does have a chemical store, as food, but falling does not use it. Falling empties the gravitational potential store.
wrong.thermal: Not quite: gravitational potential. The apple is not getting cooler as it falls; it is getting lower.

idk.hint: The apple starts high up. Which store is for raised things?

steps.answerWhy: The apple starts high up, so energy leaves its gravitational potential store.

steps.question: A child slides down a slide, and the slide gets warm. Which sentence describes the warming best?

options.text: Energy is transferred mechanically, by rubbing, from the child's gravitational potential store to the thermal store of the slide
Energy is transferred by heating from the thermal store of the slide to the child's kinetic store
Energy is transferred electrically from the child's chemical store to the thermal store of the slide

steps.right: Yes: it names the pathway, the store the energy leaves and the store it goes into. The child loses height, and rubbing transfers some of that energy to the slide.

wrong.other: Not quite. The rubbing force transfers energy mechanically from the child's gravitational potential store to the thermal store of the slide.
wrong.reverse: Not quite: the other way round. The slide warms up, so energy goes into its thermal store, from the child's gravitational potential store, by the rubbing force.
wrong.elec: Not quite: there is no current in a slide. The rubbing force transfers energy mechanically from the child's gravitational potential store to the thermal store of the slide.

idk.hint: The child loses height, and the slide warms up. Which sentence has energy leaving the store for height and going into the slide's thermal store?

steps.answerWhy: The rubbing force transfers energy mechanically from the child's gravitational potential store to the thermal store of the slide.

steps.prompt: In one line: what are the four pathways energy can be transferred by?
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: energy is transferred mechanically by a force, electrically by a current, by heating, or by radiation.

keyPoints.heading: Conservation of energy — the rule that never breaks

steps.text: Now the most important rule about energy. Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be moved from store to store, or spread out. This rule is called the law of conservation of energy.

Picture a book pushed off a table. As it falls, energy moves from its gravitational potential store to its kinetic store. When it hits the floor, the bang carries some away as sound, and in the end the floor and the air get a tiny bit warmer.
For the falling book, add up the energy at the end and you get the same total as at the start.
A system is the object, or group of objects, you are looking at: here, the book, the floor and the air around them.
A system that no energy can get into or out of is called a closed system. In a closed system, the total energy never changes.

steps.question: A torch battery goes flat. What has happened to the energy that was in its chemical store?

options.text: It went to other stores, mostly the thermal store of the room around it
It has been used up and is gone
It is still inside the battery

steps.right: Yes. The energy went by light and heating into the thermal store of the room. The battery runs down, but the energy still exists.

wrong.other: Not quite. The energy went to other stores, mostly the thermal store of the surroundings.
wrong.usedup: Not quite: energy is never destroyed. The battery's chemical store has emptied, and the energy went by light and heating into the thermal store of the room. The battery runs down; the energy does not.
wrong.charge: Not quite: the battery is flat, so its chemical store has emptied. The current carried the energy to the bulb, which sent it out by light and heating, and in the end it warms the room.

idk.hint: Energy cannot be destroyed, so it has gone somewhere. The torch gave out light and got warm. Which button says where?

steps.answerWhy: Energy cannot be destroyed: it went by light and heating into the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.text: Another example: a ball hits a wall and stops. Its kinetic store falls to zero, and the thermal stores of the ball and the wall rise: both get very slightly warmer.

steps.question: Water is boiled in an electric kettle. Which store of the water rises?
steps.right: Yes: the water gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

wrong.other: Not quite: the water gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: the water does swirl as it boils, but that is small. The big change is that it gets much hotter, so its thermal store rises.
wrong.chemical: Not quite: boiling water is not a fuel or a food. It gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

idk.hint: The water gets hotter. Which store depends on how hot something is?

steps.answerWhy: The water gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

steps.question: A moving trolley rolls to a stop on a carpet. Which describes it best?

options.text: Its kinetic store emptied into thermal stores by rubbing
It ran out of force as it rolled over the carpet
The carpet destroyed its energy as it slowed it down

steps.right: Yes. Rubbing on the carpet transferred the energy from the trolley's kinetic store to thermal stores.

wrong.other: Not quite. Its kinetic store emptied into the thermal stores of the trolley, carpet and air.
wrong.force: Not quite: a moving thing does not carry force. It has energy in its kinetic store, and rubbing on the carpet transferred that to the thermal stores of the trolley, carpet and air.
wrong.destroyed: Not quite: energy is never destroyed. Rubbing on the carpet moved it from the trolley's kinetic store to the thermal stores of the trolley, carpet and air.

idk.hint: Energy cannot be destroyed. When things rub, they get a little warmer. Which button says that?

steps.answerWhy: Rubbing on the carpet moved the energy from the kinetic store to the thermal stores of the trolley, carpet and air.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does the law of conservation of energy say?
points: energy cannot be created or destroyed
it can only be transferred from store to store
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another.

keyPoints.heading: Dissipation — where useful energy goes to die

steps.text: In every real machine, some energy goes where you do not want it. A car engine is meant to make the car move, but it also gets hot and makes a noise.
The energy that does the job you want is called useful energy. For a car engine, it is the energy that goes into the car's kinetic store.
Energy that goes anywhere else is called wasted energy. For the car, wasted energy is what heats up the engine and makes the noise.

Wasted energy nearly always ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings, warming the air a tiny bit. It spreads out so thinly that nobody can use it again. Scientists say it is dissipated: spread out and no longer useful.
The picture shows a torch. Energy leaves the battery's chemical store electrically. The bulb sends out useful energy by radiation, as light, and wasted energy by heating.

steps.question: A TV is meant to give out light and sound, but its back gets warm. What is the energy that warms the back of the TV?

options.text: Wasted energy, dissipated to the surroundings

steps.right: Yes. A TV's job is light and sound, so the energy that warms its back is wasted, and it is dissipated to the surroundings.

wrong.other: Not quite. A TV's job is light and sound, so warming its back is wasted energy, dissipated to the surroundings.
wrong.useful: Not quite. A TV's job is light and sound, so the energy that only warms its back is wasted energy, dissipated to the surroundings.
wrong.destroyed: Not quite: the energy still exists. The energy that warms the TV is wasted energy, dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

idk.hint: A TV's job is to give light and sound. Is warming its back part of that job?

steps.answerWhy: A TV's job is light and sound, so the energy that warms its back is wasted, dissipated to the surroundings.

steps.question: A hot drink cools down in a room. Can the energy that left it be used to heat the drink back up?

options.text: No: it is spread thinly through the room, warming it only a tiny bit
Yes: it is all still in the room, so the room will heat the drink again
Yes, if you wait long enough

steps.right: Right: the energy still exists, but it is spread so thinly through the room that it cannot warm the drink again. That is what dissipated means.

wrong.other: Not quite: no. The energy is spread so thinly through the room that it cannot warm the drink again.
wrong.room: Not quite: the energy is still in the room, but spread so thinly that the room is only a tiny bit warmer. A slightly warm room cannot heat a drink back up.
wrong.fridge: Not quite: waiting will not help. The drink ends up at room temperature, and the energy that left it stays spread thinly through the room.

idk.hint: The room only gets a tiny bit warmer. Can a room that is only a tiny bit warmer heat up a drink?

steps.answerWhy: The energy is spread so thinly through the room that it cannot heat the drink again: it is dissipated.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does it mean when energy is dissipated?
points: it spreads out into the surroundings
so it is no longer useful
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: dissipated energy has spread out into the surroundings, so it is no longer useful.

steps.text: Last part: a way to draw where energy goes. A Sankey diagram is an arrow diagram in which the width of each arrow shows how much energy it carries.
Here is one for a lamp. 100 J goes in on the left. 15 J carries on to the right as light: the useful energy. 85 J bends down: wasted, by heating the surroundings. 15 J + 85 J = 100 J.

steps.question: A different lamp takes in 60 J and gives out 12 J of light. How many joules are wasted?
steps.right: Yes: 48 J. Wasted = total in − useful out = 60 − 12 = 48 J.

wrong.other: Not quite: 48 J. Wasted = total in − useful out = 60 − 12 = 48 J.
wrong.add: Not quite: 48 J. The energy out cannot be more than the energy in. Take the useful part away: 60 − 12 = 48 J.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 48 J. To find the wasted energy, subtract: 60 − 12 = 48 J.

idk.hint: All 60 J has to go somewhere: 12 J as light, and the rest wasted. Work out 60 − 12.

steps.answerWhy: Wasted = total in − useful out = 60 − 12 = 48 J.

steps.question: In the first lamp's Sankey diagram, with 100 J going in, which arrow is wider?

options.text: The wasted arrow, because more energy is wasted
The useful arrow, because it is the important one

steps.right: Yes: 85 J is wasted and only 15 J is useful, so the wasted arrow is much wider. The width shows the amount of energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: the wasted arrow. The width shows the amount of energy, and 85 J is more than 15 J.
wrong.useful: Not quite: the width shows the amount of energy, not how important it is. 85 J is wasted and 15 J is useful, so the wasted arrow is wider.
wrong.same: Not quite: each arrow's width shows its own amount. 85 J is more than 15 J, so the wasted arrow is wider.

idk.hint: The width of an arrow shows how much energy it carries. Which carries more, 85 J or 15 J?

steps.answerWhy: The width shows the amount of energy, and 85 J wasted is more than 15 J useful, so the wasted arrow is wider.

steps.text: Efficiency is the fraction of the energy put in that does a useful job. Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy: the useful energy out divided by all the energy put in, both in joules.
For the lamp: 15 ÷ 100 = 0.15. Multiply by 100 to make a percentage: 15%.
Efficiency has no unit, because it is joules divided by joules.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A motor is supplied with 400 J. It transfers 300 J usefully to a kinetic store. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
steps: Write the equation: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy.

steps.question: Your turn. A kettle takes in 2000 J, and 1800 J goes into the water's thermal store. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?

wrong.other: Not quite: 90%. Efficiency = 1800 ÷ 2000 = 0.9, which is 90%.
wrong.decimal: Nearly: 0.9 is the efficiency as a decimal. As a percentage, multiply by 100: 90%.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 90%. Divide the useful energy by the total: 1800 ÷ 2000 = 0.9, which is 90%.

idk.hint: Divide the useful energy, 1800, by the total, 2000. Then multiply by 100.

steps.question: Someone works out that a machine has an efficiency of 120%. What does that tell you?

options.text: They made a mistake: no machine gets out more useful energy than goes in

steps.right: Yes. Energy cannot be created, so an efficiency is never more than 100% (or 1). Over 100% usually means dividing the wrong way round.

wrong.other: Not quite. An efficiency over 100% is always a mistake, because energy cannot be created.
wrong.good: Not quite: over 100% is impossible. The useful energy out can never be more than the energy in, so it is a mistake, usually dividing the wrong way round.
wrong.makes: Not quite: energy cannot be created, so no machine makes extra. Over 100% is a mistake, usually dividing the wrong way round.

idk.hint: Can a machine give out more energy than is put in?

steps.answerWhy: Energy cannot be created, so an efficiency is never more than 100% (or 1).

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you work out efficiency?
points: useful output energy divided by total input energy
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy, times 100 for a percentage.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: which store holds energy in a stretched rubber band?
steps.right: Yes: stretched things have energy in their elastic potential store.

wrong.other: Not quite: elastic potential, the store for stretched or squashed things.

steps.answerWhy: Stretched things have energy in their elastic potential store.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: which pathway carries energy from the Sun to the Earth?
steps.right: Yes: by radiation, as light and infrared waves.

wrong.other: Not quite: by radiation, as light and infrared waves.

steps.answerWhy: Energy reaches the Earth from the Sun by radiation, as light and infrared.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: which statement is true?

options.text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed
Energy is used up when a battery goes flat

steps.right: Yes: that is the law of conservation of energy.

wrong.other: Not quite. Energy cannot be created or destroyed: that is the law of conservation of energy.
wrong.w1: Not quite: a power station does not create energy; it transfers it from a fuel or another store. Energy cannot be created or destroyed.
wrong.w2: Not quite: the battery runs down, but its energy is not used up. It moves to other stores, mostly the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.answerWhy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed: the law of conservation of energy.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: a device takes in 200 J and gives out 50 J usefully. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?

wrong.decimal: Nearly: 0.25 is the efficiency as a decimal. As a percentage, multiply by 100: 25%.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: where does most wasted energy end up?

options.text: The thermal store of the surroundings
The chemical store of the device
The kinetic store of the device

steps.right: Yes: it is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.answerWhy: Wasted energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: a ball rolls along the floor and stops. An exam asks you to describe the energy changes. Which answer scores?

options.text: Energy is transferred mechanically, by friction, from the ball's kinetic store to the thermal stores of the floor and air
The ball's energy is used up by the floor

steps.right: Yes: the pathway, the store the energy leaves and the store it goes into.

wrong.other: Not quite. Name the pathway and both stores: energy is transferred mechanically, by friction, from the ball's kinetic store to the thermal stores of the floor and air.
wrong.w2: Not quite: energy is never used up. Energy is transferred mechanically, by friction, from the ball's kinetic store to the thermal stores of the floor and air.

steps.answerWhy: Energy is transferred mechanically, by friction, from the ball's kinetic store to the thermal stores of the floor and air.
